full_judgment:
6. The learned Counsel for the appellant submits that the instant suit was barred by limitation, the High Court Division and the appellate Court erred in law in holding that the plaintiffs will be entitled to get sixty years after 18 years of amendment of Bangol Tenancy Act for redemption. He submits that the instant mortgage was "bemedi" mortgage the period of redemption is sixty years from the date of mort-gage and the said period expired in 1962, the learned Courts below erred in law in not dismissing the suit on the ground of limitation. 

 11. That is, outstanding characteristic of a simple mortgage is that possession is not to be delivered to the mortgagee. In the mortgage deed there was stipulation that against the loan, the mortgagor would pay interest of tk. 6 and 4 annas in every month to the mortgagee. If the mortgagor fails to pay interest he would deliver possession of the disputed property to the mortgagee, which did not convert the simple mortgage into a usufructuary mortgage. From the contents of the mortgage deed and nature of the mortgage it appears that instant mortgage was a simple mortgage. The provision of section 26B of the Bengal Tenancy Act which was introducted by the amending Act of 1938 is applicable in the case of usufructuary mortgage and in that case two remedies were open for the mortgagor to get redress which were (i) filing application under section 26B of the Bengol Tenancy Act or (2) by filing a regular suit for redemption. 

 12. Mr. Quayum in support his submission relied upon the case of Suresh Chandra Bose V. Sbohan Mridha and others reported in VII DLR page 426. In the cited case an application under section 26G of the Bengol Tenancy Act for restoration of possession of the mortgaged land which was made as far as January, 1921. Isphahani J. discussing the provision of section 26G of the Bengol Tenancy Act and 23 and 181 of the Limitation Act observed that, "in the present case the right to apply accrued as soon as section 26G of the Bengol Tenancy Act came into force in 1938 and the mortgagor had three years from the date to apply for return of the mortgaged property, which he did not do. The present application was filed as late as 18.06.1946 which is obviously time barred." The second citation of Mr. Quayum is the case of Jahur Ali Dewan and another Vs. Akram Ali Pradhania and others reported in 17 DLR page 343. In that case the plaintiff filed a suit for recovery of possession by way of redemption of the suit land. According to the plaintiffs they are entitled to recover possession of the suit land in view of the provision of section 26B of the Bengol Tenancy Act on the expiry of fifteen years of the date of the mortgage. The suit land was mortgaged in the year 1934 and the suit itself was instituted in the year 1959. Murshed C.J. observed, "since the present suit has been instituted in compliance with all the formalities and requirements of a regular suit, it must be held that it should be looked upon as a regular suit to redeem a mortgaged-property, Since it is a case of a susfractuary mortgage, it would have to be seen whether the mortgage-debt has, in fact, been paid off by the enjoyment of the usufruct of the property, even if plaintiffs are not entitled to any relief under section 26B of the Bengol Tenancy Act, such relief being barred under Article 181 of the Limitation Act. The period of limitation for an ordinary redemption suit is sixty years." 

 14. The High Court Division misinterpreting the amended provision of 26B of the Bangol Tenancy Act held that the limitation would run after 18 years of the said amendment, that is, from 22.02.1944. In the instant case the limitation for redemption would run as per provision of Article 148 of the Limitation Act, that is, the plaintiffs ought to have filed the suit for redemption or recovery of possession within 60 years from 22.02.1902 which has expired on 21.02.1962. The courts below committed error of law in not holding that the instant suit was barred by limitation.
